blocks.text: A container is an ordinary host process with a restricted view of the system (namespaces) and capped resources (cgroups), sharing the host kernel. A VM runs its own guest kernel on virtual hardware provided by a hypervisor.

rows: Linux containers need a Linux kernel

blocks.text:
$ docker run -d --name web nginx:1.27
$ ps -ef | grep "nginx: master"      # visible on the host with a host PID; PID 1 inside

items: Kernel features (cgroup v2, io_uring, eBPF) come from the host, not the image. "FROM ubuntu:24.04" doesn't bring Ubuntu's kernel.
Weaker boundary: a kernel exploit is a potential escape for every container on the host. Multi-tenant platforms add gVisor, Kata Containers or Firecracker.
GPUs: the driver lives on the host; the image carries only the CUDA userland (NVIDIA Container Toolkit bridges them).

blocks.text: Q: "Container vs VM?" A: "A container is a process isolated by namespaces and limited by cgroups on the shared host kernel; a VM virtualizes hardware and boots its own kernel. Containers win on startup and density, VMs on isolation."

items: Container = process + namespaces + cgroups on the host kernel.
No guest kernel: kernel behavior and bugs come from the host.
Shared kernel means a weaker security boundary than a VM.
Linux containers on macOS/Windows require a Linux VM.
